stories.topic: From Carrying Marx to Class to Discovering Spontaneous Order
stories.summary: In college Amit was fairly left-leaning and carried Marx to classes, and Marxism seemed to explain everything. That changed once he looked at the world more closely and read Friedman, Hayek and Bastiat. His second awakening came later, in adulthood. Steven Pinker's The Blank Slate opened up evolutionary psychology for him, and he went on to read everything by Dawkins, Dennett and Robert Wright. He had never believed in God, but understanding natural selection made his atheism settle into a 'comfort zone'.
stories.insight: Markets and evolution are one idea showing up in two domains: complex order that emerges bottom-up, with no central planner and no grand designer. Once you grasp one, the other clicks into place.
stories.quote: And in a sense that is a common link between what I consider the two great intellectual awakenings of my life.

stories.topic: The Scientific American Article That Hooked an Economist
stories.summary: While Ajay was an economics PhD student, he grew more and more interested in biology. The turning point was Paul Ewald's Scientific American article on the evolution of virulence. He saw deep commonalities between how economists and evolutionary biologists think about the forces that shape a system, and he 'geeked out' on books and papers. Evolution has stayed with him as a way of looking at the world ever since.
stories.insight: Economics and evolutionary biology share a mode of thought: simple competitive forces shaping a system over time. A single article from a neighbouring field can permanently rewire how you see things.
stories.quote: it just blew my mind and it was just a moment that you can't unsee.

stories.topic: How Newton Made Room for God
stories.summary: People once believed God personally chose the exact location and orbit of Jupiter. Newton's reconciliation was that God made universal laws like F = GMm/r², set the system going and let it whirl along, and humans find joy in deciphering that machine. Ajay offers a parallel for biology. All you need is to reach self-replicating molecules. After that, sexual reproduction, sexual selection and ever-escalating complexity are more or less inevitable, so a believer could place God at that initialization, or all the way back at the Big Bang.
stories.insight: Science need not evict faith. It moves the designer's role from tinkering with every detail to setting the laws or initial conditions. Natural selection, like gravity, then runs on its own.
stories.quote: God made the laws. And He got a system going, and then the system whirled along. And we are humble and joyous at deciphering the works of God.

stories.topic: A Friend Who Thought Gym Gains Are Heritable
stories.summary: A friend told Amit that if he worked out well and lived a disciplined life, his kid could inherit those properties. Amit replied that the child can pick up the habits by watching him, but they won't be in his DNA. The belief is Lamarckism: the idea that changes you make in your lifetime, like a blacksmith's strong arms, pass on through your genes. It was common in the 19th century, before genetics was understood, and we now know there is nothing to it.
stories.insight: Folk Lamarckism still feels intuitive. Behaviour you adopt in your lifetime doesn't rewrite the DNA you pass on. What your children get from your discipline travels through example, which means culture.
stories.quote: No, he can pick them up from you by watching you do all those things. But they're not gonna be part of his DNA.

stories.topic: Dara Singh's Daughter and a Father's Lesson in Biology
stories.summary: When Ajay was growing up, his sister had a classmate who was the daughter of the wrestler Dara Singh, and she was very strong. Ajay's father used her to teach his children about Lamarckism. Some nature was transmitted, but it was not the bodybuilding Dara Singh had done. His strength was in his genes at birth. On top of that, she grew up in a household that prized physicality and probably exercised a lot.
stories.insight: What looks like inherited talent is genes plus a correlated upbringing, never the parent's acquired gains. A good childhood example can become lifelong intellectual scaffolding.
stories.quote: it is not the bodybuilding that Dara Singh did in order to become a successful wrestler. It was there in his genes at birth

stories.topic: Kapil Dev on How to Get Another Kapil Dev
stories.summary: Near the end of his career, Kapil Dev was asked mournfully by a reporter at a press conference: 'Sir, you will retire soon, how can we get another Kapil Dev?' Kapil replied that his father was dead and his mother was too old. Amit recalled it right after the discussion of what is and isn't inherited.
stories.insight: A deadpan reminder that exceptional talent can't be manufactured on demand. Part of what made him came from his parents, and that is not a recipe anyone can repeat.
stories.quote: my father is dead, my mother is too old.

stories.topic: Sickle Cell, Thalassemia and the Malaria Trade-off
stories.summary: In sickle cell anemia, red blood cells collapse into a sickle shape when the heart is pushed hard, so a person running from a leopard can abruptly crash. Thalassemia also involves malfunctioning red blood cells. For a long time it seemed these traits should have died out. Scientists later understood that they are selected for where malaria is common. The malaria plasmodium hides inside red blood cells, beyond the reach of the immune system, and multiplies there. Sickling makes the plasmodium's survival much harder. Evolution struck a balance between peak cardiac capability and malaria survival, which is why entire communities in India carry these traits.
stories.insight: An apparent defect can be a defence against a threat you weren't looking at. Evolution doesn't perfect single traits. It trades them off against the real dangers of a particular environment.
stories.quote: It turns out that thalassemia and sickle cell anemia are selected for in environments with malaria.

stories.topic: Lactase Persistence and the Milk Cultures
stories.summary: All mammal infants make lactase to digest the lactose in milk, and they lose the ability as they grow up. About 7,000 to 8,000 years ago, a mutation on the border between Bulgaria and Turkey let adults keep making lactase. Milk became high-quality adult nutrition. Whole cow-owning, cow-herding cultures grew around it, and its carriers reproduced well and conquered faraway lands, including northern India. In India, the gene is still far more common in the north, where those invasions happened, than in the south.
stories.insight: Biology and culture co-evolve. A mutation unlocks a resource, culture builds itself around exploiting it, and together they produce enormous genetic success that you can still trace on a map.
stories.quote: there was a mutation that was selected by natural selection and then the culture turned around and exploited that.

stories.topic: The Deep-Sea Diving Women of Jeju Island
stories.summary: On Korea's Jeju Island, diving into the deep sea (for pearls, as Ajay puts it) has been the main livelihood for hundreds of years. Women better able to hold their breath, process oxygen and cope with pressure came back with the catch. Those less adapted had accidents and died. Over centuries the population developed remarkable physical adaptations for diving, much as Himalayan Sherpas cope with low oxygen. Amit added that the world's top long-distance runners come from East Africa, with altitude, terrain and culture amplifying the effect.
stories.insight: Natural selection is not only ancient history. A livelihood that applies steady pressure over centuries can visibly shape a population's biology.
stories.quote: over hundreds of years these women have developed remarkable physical adaptations through which they are better able to engage in deep sea diving

stories.topic: How the Industrial Revolution Turned Britain's Moths Black
stories.summary: British moths were originally white or off-white. Then poor-quality coal furnaces covered buildings in black soot, and white moths resting on black walls became easy prey for birds. Darker mutants survived better, and within a couple of decades industrial England's moths had turned black. The example played a big role in the earliest debates over evolution. Amit spelled out the mechanism: a few random dark mutants always exist, and the environment decides who survives. The same process explains mosquitoes resistant to insecticides and bacteria resistant to antibiotics. Nothing is being 'learned'; rare resistant mutants simply survive and multiply.
stories.insight: Evolution can play out in front of your eyes when selection pressure is strong. The environment does the choosing among random variations that already exist.
stories.quote: within a couple of decades the moths of industrial revolution England turned black.

stories.topic: DDT Fogging, Antibiotic Courses and Breeding Superbugs
stories.summary: When a single housing colony does DDT fogging, neighbouring buildings get a partial dose. The mosquitoes that survive it are the ones with some resistance, so each round ratchets the population toward complete resistance. Antibiotics fail the same way. A full course drives pathogens down to very low counts so the immune system can finish them off. But people feel better within two or three weeks and stop early, which leaves the most resistant pathogens alive to surge back. Each imperfect cycle breeds antimicrobial resistance. Amit called it evolutionary theory meeting human hubris.
stories.insight: Partial doses are worse than useless because they actively select for resistance. Individual incentives (fog just my colony, stop when I feel fine) erode collective assets, so this has to be handled as a population-scale public health problem.
stories.quote: But at the level of a society, one by one we lose our silver bullets.

stories.topic: Cholera in East Bengal vs West Bengal
stories.summary: In the early years after independence, West Bengal improved its drinking water and reduced fecal contamination, while East Bengal did not. Where contaminated water guaranteed transmission, cholera had no reason to keep its host alive. It killed fast, driving diarrhea into the water supply. Where transmission got harder, cholera strains evolved toward lower virulence. Ajay applies the same logic to COVID. In crowded settings like Bombay's suburban trains or the Maha Kumbh, the most rapacious strains win. Masking and distancing push the virus toward mildness.
stories.insight: Public health measures do more than block spread. They change the evolutionary incentives of the pathogen itself, so better sanitation can make a disease less deadly.
stories.quote: the incentives of the cholera changed and the strains of cholera evolved to have lower levels of virulence.

stories.topic: The 1944 Amsterdam Famine and Its Children
stories.summary: In 1944, after a rebellion around Amsterdam, the Nazis cut off the roads to starve the city as punishment. The Allies airdropped food, but there was a terrible famine. Years later, scientists studied children who were exposed to the famine in varying degrees between conception and birth, comparing them with those born before and after. Those exposed to starvation in the womb had a much higher propensity to obesity, hoarding food more desperately, and the effect persisted for several generations.
stories.insight: Same DNA, different outcome. Early environment changes how genes are expressed, and that is how nurture physically turns nature's knobs.
stories.quote: The children that were born out of their exposure to starvation had much more of a propensity to obesity.

recommendations.creator: Paul Ewald
recommendations.context: Ajay names it as the turning point of his PhD years and later lays out its argument, using cholera and COVID as examples. Linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: It blew his mind. The idea that how easily a pathogen spreads determines how deadly it evolves to be is a lens you can't unsee.

recommendations.creator: Matt Ridley
recommendations.context: Raised when Ajay linked evolution to spontaneous order. It is also on the show notes' further reading list.
recommendations.reason: It shows the same bottom-up process, with no central planner and no grand designer, behind natural selection, languages, society and economies. That bridges Amit's two intellectual awakenings.

recommendations.item: The Evolution of Everything (Episode 96 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Matt Ridley)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentions doing an episode with Matt Ridley on the book. Linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: The long-form conversation on spontaneous order across biology, culture and markets.

recommendations.creator: Leonard Read
recommendations.context: Ajay's levels-of-understanding analogy: level one is the person who 'gets I, Pencil'. Linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: It makes you see how mind-boggling it is to make even a pencil, which is the first step toward understanding that such complexity comes from self-organizing systems, not central planning.

recommendations.creator: Steven Pinker
recommendations.context: Amit's entry point into natural selection in adulthood. On the further reading list.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a masterpiece and his window into evolutionary psychology and natural selection.

recommendations.creator: Richard Dawkins
recommendations.context: Discussed in the segment on semantic confusion. On the further reading list.
recommendations.reason: A landmark book with a 'fantastic metaphor'. Read carefully rather than literally, selfish-gene reasoning ends up explaining why humans are altruistic.

recommendations.creator: Richard Dawkins
recommendations.context: On the show notes' further reading list. Amit says he read everything by Dawkins, and the episode discusses Paley's watchmaker argument.
recommendations.reason: One of the books the hosts learned the subject from. It pairs with the episode's point that intricate design can arise without a designer.

recommendations.creator: Daniel Dennett
recommendations.context: On the further reading list. Ajay quotes Dennett calling evolutionary theory a 'universal acid', and Amit read everything by Dennett.
recommendations.reason: One of the core books the hosts learned evolution from, by the thinker who framed it as an idea that dissolves simple preconceptions.

recommendations.creator: Robert Wright
recommendations.context: Robert Wright is among the authors Amit read after The Blank Slate. On the further reading list.
recommendations.reason: Part of the core reading through which Amit came to understand natural selection and evolutionary psychology.

recommendations.creator: Donald Symons
recommendations.context: Cited for the observation that science expands knowledge but not language, and as part of Amit's early reading. On the further reading list.
recommendations.reason: Formative for Amit's understanding of how and why men and women evolved differently. He says A Billion Wicked Thoughts later confirmed its arguments with data.

recommendations.creator: Robert Axelrod
recommendations.context: Raised when the hosts explain why selfish-gene logic leads to altruism. On the further reading list.
recommendations.reason: Uses game theory and natural selection to show why we evolved to cooperate and even sacrifice for the tribe, which makes sense from the gene's point of view.

recommendations.creator: Ogi Ogas and Sai Gaddam
recommendations.context: Recommended to Amit by a friend, Aditi, after the alt-data episode (EIE 118). It is the basis for next week's episode on sexual preferences, and Amit reads its passage on taste and culture in this one.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a brilliant book and a masterpiece. It uses hard data on anonymized internet behaviour to show what men and women want, explains why through natural selection, and confirms the arguments of Symons, Buss, Miller and Pinker.

recommendations.creator: Chinmay Tumbe
recommendations.context: Mentioned during the discussion of how pathogen virulence evolves. Linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: Highlights that past pandemics ended not because we eliminated the strain but because it evolved toward the least virulent form. That is why Amit was confident COVID would become something we live with.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit refers to his episode with Chinmay Tumbe on The Age of Pandemics. Linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: The deeper conversation on the history of pandemics and how they play out.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The episode grows out of the course's 'Know Thyself' webinars on understanding your evolutionary hardwiring and your cultural shaping.
recommendations.reason: Teaches self-knowledge through understanding how evolution and culture shaped you, which is the theme of this episode.

core_ideas.concept: Evolution as the Ultimate Spontaneous Order
core_ideas.explanation: Dennett called evolutionary theory a 'universal acid' that strips away simple preconceptions. Evolution has no central planner, no teleology and no objective, yet it produces the human eye and the eagle's eye. Ajay's moral: when you marvel at such design and feel the engineer's urge to plan and control, remember that it came from an uncontrolled, self-organizing system. That is an argument against central planning and industrial policy.
core_ideas.quote: Evolution is the ultimate success story of spontaneous order.

core_ideas.concept: The Pencil Ladder: Levels of Understanding Complexity
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's four levels. Level zero thinks pencils are easy to make. Level one 'gets I, Pencil' and is amazed at how much it takes. Level two concludes something this complex needs a central committee directing the aluminium and steel. The highest level understands that self-organizing systems produce pencils without anyone in charge. Faced with nature's complexity, the same trap is to assume a designer.
core_ideas.quote: the highest level where you have arrived in understanding the world is to understand that we can actually make pencils out of thin air, and it's called a self organizing system.

core_ideas.explanation: William Paley argued that a watch found on a beach, unlike a stone, implies a watchmaker, and so the intricacy of the human eye implies God. Natural selection shows that random variation plus selection can produce such intricacy bottom-up. That makes the metaphorical watchmaker unnecessary, though not impossible: a believer can say God created the process itself. Natural selection is independent of the question of God and of where morality comes from.
core_ideas.quote: Darwin made the existence of a metaphorical watchmaker irrelevant.

core_ideas.explanation: Hume's is-ought fallacy derives a prescription from a description. G.E. Moore's naturalistic fallacy defines 'good' as 'natural'. Bigots once called homosexuality unnatural and therefore wrong, which committed the fallacy and was also factually false, since homosexuality occurs across many species. Amit sees the right committing it (his objection to Jordan Peterson's arguments about traditional gender roles) and the left too, when it denies any differences between men and women for fear that description implies unequal treatment. Combined with the 'man of system' engineering mindset, these fallacies fed early-20th-century eugenics, on the right and the left alike. Morality is ours to decide through reason; nature can constrain or enable, but it shouldn't dictate.
core_ideas.quote: a description of something doesn't imply a prescription of anything

core_ideas.concept: Nature Gives You Knobs, Nurture Turns Them
core_ideas.explanation: Nature versus nurture is a false binary. Amit attributes the 'knobs' line to Steven Pinker but admits he has never been able to find the source. Someone predisposed to anger may live calmly in a peaceful environment, and a placid person can be pushed to fury by a brutal life. Amit calls the Enlightenment project an exercise in deciding how we ought to live, then using culture to mitigate the hardwiring we dislike and amplify what we like.
core_ideas.quote: nature gives you knobs, nurture turns them.

core_ideas.concept: Why We Overstate the Role of Nature
core_ideas.explanation: Nature and nurture are correlated. In a hockey-playing family, the kids may inherit explosive strength and also get early coaching, praise and constant hockey talk. A talented child in such a home gets every support. Because we don't separate the two, we see 'genes for chess in this family' when a big part of what passes down is environment.
core_ideas.quote: This combination of nature and nurture makes us overstate how important nature is.

core_ideas.explanation: Our nature was tuned for prehistoric problems. Scarce food made us crave high-fat, high-sugar food. Lethal threats like a charging lion wired a hair-trigger fight-or-flight response. Life in bands of about 150 made outsiders seem dangerous, which is tribalism. Culture is the operating system on top. It can teach us to eat less sugar, to presume good faith, and to form imagined communities across the world. Amit adds that engagement-maximizing social media has accidentally amplified our tribal instincts.
core_ideas.quote: when a boss sends you a bad email, You don't have to respond like it is an attack by a tiger. In fact, you don't even have to respond right now.

core_ideas.explanation: Evolutionary explanations answer why a trait was selected for about a hundred thousand years ago. They don't describe what you consciously feel today. A man who likes youth in women isn't thinking of childbearing, and a sweet tooth isn't a conscious plan to store scarce calories. Objecting 'but I don't feel that way' confuses the two levels. Ajay adds that the conscious voice in our head is just one evolutionary adaptation among many; much of what drives us, like the circuitry that raises the heart rate, runs below awareness.
core_ideas.quote: You are not thinking about the scarcity of calories when you eat your next laddoo.

core_ideas.concept: Language Traps: Metaphor, Anthropomorphism and Teleology
core_ideas.explanation: Donald Symons noted that science expands knowledge but not language. As with 'public goods' or 'market failure' in economics, biology borrows ordinary words like messenger genes, master and slave genes, and the selfish gene, and lay readers take them literally. Genes don't 'want' anything. Read crudely, 'selfish gene' suggests people are selfish; done rigorously, the same reasoning explains human altruism. The deepest trap is teleology, the belief that evolution is aiming somewhere. It has no purpose at all.
core_ideas.quote: There is no mother evolution, and this non existent mother evolution has no objective at all

core_ideas.concept: The Bare Mechanics of Natural Selection
core_ideas.explanation: All you need are things that make copies of themselves (organisms, or even firms), variation in their traits, and finite resources to compete for. Natural selection then follows inexorably. Better resource-users leave more copies, so their traits spread and get refined to 'fiendish levels of excellence', slowly, generation after generation. There is no equality, no apex and no endpoint, just an endless competition.
core_ideas.quote: Evolution never ends. There is no apex outcome, there is no destination.

core_ideas.concept: Sex as a Variation Engine, and Sexual Selection
core_ideas.explanation: Asexual reproduction, like an amoeba splitting, yields near-copies with little variation. Sexual reproduction shuffles genes and greatly increases the variation that selection can act on. In complex creatures, mate choice becomes a second engine: traits the opposite sex prefers multiply. The springbok's huge leap when chased signals health and spare energy to mates, but it also lets the lion wait for it to land. The two engines can pull against each other.
core_ideas.quote: natural selection and sexual selection are at odds with each other

core_ideas.explanation: DNA is not a fixed program. Epigenetics studies gene expression, the way environment interacts with the genetic code to produce different outcomes. In the 1944 Amsterdam famine, exposure to starvation in the womb raised the propensity to obesity. That is not Lamarckism, which holds that behaviour you adopt in your lifetime alters the DNA you pass on. The famine didn't change anyone's DNA. It changed how existing genes were expressed.
core_ideas.quote: Epigenetics did not change the DNA of the kids who were born at that time. It merely turned the knobs differently.

core_ideas.explanation: Paul Ewald's idea is that a pathogen's virulence is tuned to how it spreads. A pathogen that must wait a long time to jump hosts does best by keeping its host alive. One that spreads easily, through dirty water or crowded air, can be rapacious. So virulence is not random. Sanitation, masking and distancing select for milder strains, and Amit notes past pandemics ended as the strains evolved toward the least virulent.
core_ideas.quote: depending on the complexity of transmission, there is an optimal level of virulence of the pathogen.

core_ideas.concept: Evolutionary Time Is Measured in Generations
core_ideas.explanation: Big mutations are usually birth defects, so change comes in tiny steps accumulated over hundreds or thousands of generations. Bacteria reproduce roughly every ten minutes and evolve at a frightening pace, which has made the immune system a major evolutionary battleground. Humans manage about one generation every 25 years, so only about 400 in 10,000 years, which barely changes anything. We are mostly the humans of 10,000 years ago living in a modernity that, on that scale, has barely begun.
core_ideas.quote: The unit of evolutionary timescale is not time, but generations

core_ideas.concept: The Brain Is Part of the Body
core_ideas.explanation: No one denies that natural selection shaped male and female bodies differently. Yet many insist that behavioural differences are purely cultural. Amit argues the brain is shaped by selection like every other organ. Cultures do magnify the worst parts of our nature, and patriarchy is real, but some differences are hardwired. The goal is to acknowledge them without concluding they justify unequal treatment.
core_ideas.quote: The brain is a part of the body, right? Every cell of our body is designed, as you pointed out, by natural selection, right? So why should we imagine that the brain is not?

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's cold open: 'Just a few moments ago, Mr. Ajay Shah was telling me about a young female mosquito which got knocked up and came looking for mammalian proteins, but unfortunately collided with my jeans pants. So nothing much is happening there.'
After Ajay recites F = GMm/r² and builds his pencil analogy, Amit asks: 'How many equations do you know by heart, by the way?'
Amit illustrating the anger knob: your life could be nasty, brutish and hard, and 'you keep meeting Bengali economists and you can't help shouting at them.'
Ajay, self-aware: 'gentle readers who are tired and bored of Everything is Everything, where we say the same lines over and over. We are large, we contain multitudes.'
After the shoot moved indoors because of rain, Amit: 'under the pressure of natural selection, my shirt changed into a hoodie. Isn't it miraculous how these things work?'
On the springbok, whose showy leaps for mates let the lion wait for it to land, Amit: 'I guess evolution among the springboks could then be called a race to the top.'
Amit on the Amsterdam famine babies: the famine turned the sweetness knob up full, and 'those kids ended up, you know, eating a lot of laddoos, if laddoos were ever in Amsterdam.'
On sickle cell's trade-off between outrunning a leopard and surviving malaria, Amit: 'I have a title for the short story. The Lion and the Mosquito.' Ajay corrects: 'The Lion or the Mosquito.'
Amit on the losers of the lactase story: lactose-intolerant people without the gene who live in a culture that keeps nagging them, in Hindi, about why they don't drink milk every day.

Ajay explaining that a too-virulent pathogen can't get copies out to others: 'Not that he's thinking, this is just evolutionary theory.' Amit: 'Not that he's a he.' Ajay: 'in fact, many of them have no gender.'

Amit, right after the chapter on semantics: 'I'm really glad that we had that chapter where we spoke about the importance of semantics, because here you are talking about the incentives of COVID virus.'
On why this became a two-parter: 'this will become like a Seen and the Unseen eight-hour episode if we try to combine it all into one thing.'
Amit's closing pun after Ajay's ode to the human and eagle eye: 'The only kind of eye I don't like, Ajay, is the I in ego.'

Douglas Adams, quoted by Amit on natural selection: 'The awe it inspired in me made the awe that people talk about in respect of religious experience seem, frankly, silly beside it. I take the awe of understanding over the awe of ignorance any day.'

Ghiselin, quoted by Amit on why Darwin's cosmology was so hard to accept: 'A world populated by organisms striving to no end, but rather playing ridiculous sexual games. A world in which the brain is itself an extension of the gonads simply cannot be reconciled with the old way of thinking.'

Eugenics wasn't only Hitler's project: Amit notes that H.G. Wells and George Bernard Shaw, both Fabian socialists and both inspirations for Nehru, also believed in it. He sees it as the naturalistic fallacy combined with Adam Smith's 'man of system'.
Neuroscientist Paul MacLean's list of misleading biology jargon: genes as 'messengers', 'promoters', 'operators', 'master genes' and 'slave genes'.
Ogi Ogas and Sai Gaddam on culture shaping taste: 'We can learn to appreciate food that is bitter, like coffee or olives, but no culture enjoys cinnamon sprinkled feces.'
Ajay on how recent the rule of law is in evolutionary terms: 'the Magna Carta is 1215, it's like blink of an eye. It was only the day before yesterday that the Magna Carta happened.'
The episode's framing comes from the Ancient Greek exhortation 'Know thyself', the theme of the 'Know Thyself' webinars in their Life Lessons course.
